blocks.text: Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.
It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.
I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:
Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.
Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

blocks.text: There are decades where nothing happens, and there are weeks when decades happen. The CEO and founder of Nvidia just experienced the latter, as did many in tech, media, and government. I have a variety of thoughts after spending the past several days reading and recording podcasts about these (figurative and literal) affairs, but let me express one unpopular sentiment at the outset: what happened to Jensen Huang this week is tragic and depressing.

I have a disease that makes me sympathetic to almost anyone who ends up on the wrong end of viral outrage and panic, and unfortunately it’s flaring up again. Huang is one of the greatest CEOs in American history. He’s still hyper competent, he’s been incredibly important to the growth of the AI ecosystem, and frankly, he’s among the most sane of the contemporary tech leaders we have on offer. His fall from grace has been not only stunning but seemingly coordinated. It’s been painful to watch on a human level, and of course it has ominous implications for the tech industry. Regardless, though: what’s done is done. Huang’s reputation has been irreparably harmed, his wife and family have been humiliated over the past two weeks, and he just lost control of the world-conquering company that he founded 33 years ago, immediately throwing Nvidia’s future into a world of post-Jobsian uncertainty.

It’s an incredible coup for the Ministry of State Security if this was all a Chinese op, but honestly, I’m not convinced it was. That’s point number two. The entire media establishment and most of our government seem to have taken it as a given that Alice Huang was a spy for the MSS, but a) the sourcing there is based entirely on the vague and classified claims of intelligence services who despise Huang, while b) “spy for the MSS” can mean different things. Was she a 43-year-old operative trained by the MSS to honeypot powerful executives and obtain proprietary information, or was she a businesswoman who was (like all other Chinese citizens) obligated to cooperate with the MSS when the agency discovered her affair with Jensen? I would bet on some version of the latter (“asset,” not spy), and I think it’s more likely the spy claims were invented altogether (were they?) than it is that Alice Huang was some kind of Chinese Keri Russell executing a classic sexual blackmail scheme.

All that noted, I truly don’t know. We may never know. And one thing is certain: if Alice Huang was spending billions of Chinese investor dollars to obtain high-end Nvidia hardware that was banned for export to Chinese companies and may have later been smuggled into mainland China … she was not doing that without approval from the Chinese government. So, not a CCP agent, but not not a CCP agent—and definitely not someone that Huang should have felt comfortable sleeping with. How in the world could he be so stupid?

On the other hand, should we really be surprised? Whenever Jensen Huang discusses China, I’m reminded of Upton Sinclair: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends on his not understanding it.”

Here was Huang in a recent interview with Bloomberg, answering Emily Chang’s question about engagement with China’s tech sector by saying, “We must work with them in every possible way.” Then there was Huang talking to Dwarkesh Patel in April, going viral when he angrily called it “lunacy” to worry about the CCP and PLA using advanced American hardware to execute AI cyberattacks. Equally infamous around D.C. was Huang’s conversation with Brad Gerstner last year, in which he declared that the label “China hawk” is a “badge of shame.”

Both Huang and his company were lobbying against stepped-up export controls on AI chips as early as 2022, and were (legally) circumventing the spirit and expressed purpose of those export controls with the A800 chip in 2022, the H800 in 2023, and the H20 in 2024. He’s continued to lobby against export controls throughout the Trump administration and continued his attempts to sell AI chips to both mainland China customers and China-linked entities in Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore. To be fair, of course, anyone who’s followed this space for the past several years will remember that Nvidia has been joined by Intel, Qualcomm and everyone else in the American semiconductor industry in lobbying multiple administrations against new China restrictions. Likewise, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle all have sizable footprints in Southeast Asia providing Chinese customers with access to high-end compute.

Huang has been by far the loudest and most powerful of those voices, though, and now he will fall the hardest. That’s one way to understand what happened over the past two weeks: Jensen had a giant target on his back among many in tech and government who favored stricter restrictions on Chinese chip access, his mistakes with Alice Huang and Megaspeed gave those critics ammunition, and for reasons that remain unclear (but fun to wonder about!), some of those folks have decided to pull the trigger now.

Reports of an affair with an Nvidia employee (and another one) might have been survivable three weeks ago, but certainly not after an international scandal involving sex with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was the managing director of an Nvidia customer that was likely violating U.S. laws. Once his critics got those leaks going, it was 50/50 at best that Huang kept his job, and 100 percent guaranteed that his (and Nvidia’s) credibility in Washington would be permanently decimated.

So was Huang a victim of what was ultimately an American intelligence op to leak incriminating reports that would discredit him and his policy agenda? As far as this month’s disclosures, that’s almost certainly closer to the truth than imagining a years-long honeypot scheme overseen by the MSS to influence his views. But I draw the line at calling Huang a victim, and to be clear, that’s not why I feel bad for him.

To state the obvious: Huang broke some obvious CEO rules here (don’t dip your pen in Chinese shell company ink?) and exercised horrible judgment, evidently in multiple dimensions. With Alice Huang, he also publicly lied about the affair in explicit terms, further undermining his credibility and possibly withholding material information from investors. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang told Bloomberg at the end of October.

In the weeks and months to come, I imagine Congress will be eager to find out what else Huang may have been lying about. There will be more investigations, and there is likely more to find. All such inquiries will of course begin with Megaspeed itself, a Singaporean company with a large footprint in Malaysia that was identified by Culper Research last spring as an Nvidia customer that appeared to be funded and controlled by Alibaba, circumventing U.S. export controls in full view of Huang, who visited Megaspeed “every few months” and was accompanied by representatives from Alibaba “every single time.”

Indeed, if national security secrets were not necessarily compromised by Jensen’s affair with Alice Huang (the Nvidia board’s initial construction), it’s very plausible that national security laws were broken by Megaspeed if Jensen’s customer was effectively an Alibaba cutout controlling Megaspeed data centers and purchasing export controlled chips, 50,000 of which may have made it to China. Many on Capitol Hill will argue that U.S. security interests were compromised in turn, all of which may have been downstream of Nvidia’s knowing (or unforgivably negligent) participation in the scheme (in which case Nvidia was breaking laws, too).

But again, none of this is all that surprising. As I told Bill Bishop in our episode of Sharp China this week, the potentially incriminating details of that customer relationship have been part of the public record for nearly a year, yet I never thought to mention them on the podcast. Because what was there to say? Everyone in D.C. had just accepted that this is just how Nvidia does business. Every few months there’s some new, sketchy customer highlighted by Bloomberg or the New York Times, sometimes there’s a DOJ indictment, Nvidia’s answers are never satisfying, and yet the company appeared to be bulletproof until a sex scandal shined a light on exactly how shady all of this has always been. In the years since the Biden export controls took effect, the share of Nvidia’s revenue billed to customers with Singapore addresses rose from 8% to 22%, and in July 2025, Nvidia stopped breaking out the figures altogether.

During that same period, there have been lots of anecdotes in which Nvidia is said to have bullied members of Congress and the think tank community, using donations as leverage to influence policy positions of the latter group. Bill and I have been alluding to that bare knuckles behavior on our podcast for almost four years now, and The Information highlighted the company’s broadly unpopular tactics with a new report last week:

Government officials sometimes have felt bullied in exchanges with Huang. Officials at political think tanks say Nvidia officials have threatened to cut back on their funding for expressing views the company disagrees with. And Nvidia customers say they tiptoe around certain subjects, as OpenAI has, to avoid displeasing the chip giant. […]



One semiconductor industry executive who worked with Nvidia described the company’s effort to tweak its products and sidestep the [2022] ban as giving the Biden administration “the finger” and taking the stance that it did not have to negotiate with the government.



That often adversarial attitude toward some Biden officials came not only from Huang but also from Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, according to several people who have interacted with him. Those people recalled Teter using unflattering nicknames for government officials, academics and think tank scholars he did not like.

Under Trump, Huang’s interactions with the executive branch—and the President himself—have been considerably friendlier, which invites an entirely different spectrum of criticism and lines of inquiry. What happened to scuttle the Commerce Department’s investigation of Megaspeed, and where does the DOJ investigation stand today? Did Jensen Huang urge Nvidia counsel to reach out to the government on his mistress’ behalf? Those are fair questions that I’m sure a Democrat-controlled Congress will be asking in the months to come. Meanwhile: Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom and $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund, with at least one policy flipping after Huang attended a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser and personally lobbied Trump to reinstate licenses to sell H20 chips to China (which had been allowed under Biden).

Whether attempting to buy ideological allies or bully opponents, Huang and Nvidia spent the past several years working tirelessly to subvert the democratic policy process. Lobbying is fine, but threats and bribes are not, and it always seemed to me that Nvidia tipped a bit too far over the line as they navigated D.C. That’s why the company came to be despised by most of Congress, not to mention the vast majority of the Trump Cabinet (who may be doing some of the leaking here).

Independent of whether controversial Nvidia tactics were technically legal—abrasive lobbying, redesigning high-end chips to circumvent restrictions, moving Chinese sales offshore—there is also the question of whether any of this was wise. While reaping the unbelievable rewards of U.S. markets, laws, and customers, Nvidia has not really behaved like an American company that’s answerable to the American government. Instead, Huang continued selling chips to China at all costs and sought to substitute his own judgment for that of Congress, the White House, and practically the entire U.S. intelligence community. Those are some of the worst enemies you can possibly create, and it all reminds me a little bit of Anthropic’s battle with the Trump administration, when Dario Amodei was operating from the position that because he had a signed contract and had invented the world-changing technology at issue, he could dictate to the U.S. military how it should and shouldn’t be deployed. Good luck with that, a student of history might say.

Meanwhile, Ben Thompson has laid out an elegant case for selling high-end chips to China, but it has to be said that Jensen himself never came close to approximating Ben’s humility or strategic coherence. Not only has Jensen never once advocated for restricting the sale of semiconductor equipment to China (as Ben did), but his public answers on incredibly difficult chip questions have been evasive …
…. misleading …
and outright false.

By now it should go without saying that chip diversion is systemic and Nvidia is benefiting, while yes, the U.S. is confident that high-end Nvidia chips were used to develop DeepSeek, a model that can be extended to a variety of Chinese military applications. (Another fun detail: the day after the Trump admin initially restricted the sale of H20 chips in April 2025, Huang flew to Beijing to grovel before Vice Premier He Lifeng. Nvidia later claimed that trip was scheduled regardless of the export curbs, but who really knows?)

For as brilliant and charming and tenacious as Jensen Huang may be—and as omnipotent as he may have seemed to people in the tech industry—we should be clear that his fundamental stupidity is not confined to multiple cases of workplace infidelity. Zooming out, this is a man whose technology became economically critical almost overnight, and it thrust him into a role navigating a geopolitical environment he simply could not handle. Suddenly forced to balance market-altering interests in both China and the United States, I don’t think Huang ever really understood either country’s leadership.

No one in American history has ever been less effective at winning friends in Washington than Huang and Nvidia, yes, but that was only part of the problem. What really drove the disconnect in D.C. was Jensen’s assumption that U.S. concerns about economic engagement with China were purely a function of vibes and misunderstandings, not sincerely held security principles and bitter lessons from the past 25 years. Perhaps he needed to believe all that in order to rationalize his company’s behavior, but when he said last year that China is “not an enemy” and that “China hawk” should be a badge of shame across D.C., I was immediately reminded of Biden’s Ambassador to the PRC, Nicholas Burns, who said last year, “I went to China with hawkish views and returned to the U.S. even more hawkish than when I arrived. I saw up close the true nature of its authoritarian government and its ambition to undercut the U.S. at nearly every turn.”

Almost everyone with a security clearance leaves their time in government more concerned about China than they were when they entered public service. Without reciting a laundry list of malign CCP and PLA behaviors that could support those conclusions, I will only note that Huang was in China constantly and he seemed to be blind to all of them. Conversely, you hear the word “hawk” and probably imagine Donald Rumsfeld, but the China hawks in D.C. tend to be folks who are aware of a wide spectrum of security vulnerabilities and are unwilling to talk around those risks for the sake of share prices or political correctness. Their prescriptions are not always a good idea, but their signature trait is noticing problems and proposing action, not necessarily agitating for World War 3.

Huang repeatedly belittled those people with both his rhetoric and his company’s behavior, and indeed, he questioned the patriotism of anyone who dared to object. In so doing, he was waging war with not only large swaths of the U.S. security apparatus, but also the realities of Xi Jinping’s China that would inevitably make it impossible to sustain his position without looking naive, selfish, and unforgivably reckless.

So why did I feel bad for Huang this week? Because I’m a sap, first of all, and I’m never rooting for anyone’s public disgrace. But also because this is a man who seemed incapable of recognizing how and why this story might eventually end horribly for him. And now that we’re here, I can’t help but wince at just how much worse it’s going to get.

articles.summary: Microsoft, and Its Customers, Are Suffering a Global Cloud Outage

blocks.text: Shortly after detecting the outage, Microsoft confirmed that the main issue was “a portion of infrastructure” that “is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions.” This was not caused by increased traffic, Microsoft said, but “a problem that’s causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

Once it became clear that the failed health checks were to blame, Microsoft said it took steps to prevent additional server outages while validating alternate health check methods. But four hours later, the company admitted that it was still in the weeds.

“We’re opening all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” Microsoft said. “We found a core process on affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, causing capacity loss. To validate a potential recovery, we’re isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.”

Even small wins seemed to turn into new setbacks. As Microsoft worked to resolve the issue, some of the servers it brought back online would “become unresponsive again once they receive traffic,” giving the company yet another problem to solve.

Realizing that no quick solutions were coming, Microsoft moved to extend email timeout to 48 hours. As “encouraging” recovery efforts remained ongoing, Microsoft advised users that “some intermittent issues may continue” when traffic is restored.
Users upset by Copilot, Outlook issues
Microsoft’s most recent updates confirmed that it’s seeing “broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific.”

“Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure,” Microsoft said. “Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods.”
DownDetector, which tracks user reports of service issues globally, showed that connectivity losses peaked Thursday afternoon and dropped off substantially by Friday morning.

In comments, an Outlook user described the pain of monitoring email recovery, complaining that outgoing messages seem to send fine but incoming messages are received inconsistently. Some Copilot users seemed distressed that access wasn’t restored as quickly as Outlook. One Microsoft 365 user pondered, “How many offices had people with practically nothing to do? How much has this cost?”

blocks.text: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.

Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.

It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.

One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.

Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”

Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.

Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region.Credit...Doug Mills/The New York Times
Listen
Published Nov. 12, 2026Updated Nov. 13, 2026, 9:02 a.m. ET

There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.

The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.

The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.

The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

blocks.text: Where do I start?

We have Gemini 4 Hydrogen. But it sounds like you could use Claude Sonnet 5.5. Or maybe 5.4; it really depends. Have you tried Opus? We have Opus 5.2 right now. It's similar to Fable 5.2, but better for day-to-day work. It's not quite as powerful as Mythos 5.2, though. I hear the gap will narrow eventually. Opus scores 94.8 on a benchmark, while Mythos gets 96.1. Fable is a respectable 92.7, assuming you don't ask it to do anything too ambitious.

Have you tried the Chinese models? DeepSeek is pretty good. You might want to start with the R1 family to test the waters before moving on to V4. Personally, I'm a Flash kind of guy, but Pro is pretty good too. The crowd favorite is GLM these days. You've got to try 5.3 Flash. Its Mixture-of-Experts architecture is state of the art, in my opinion. It scores an impressive 87.3 on the Benchmark Performance Index.

But let's be serious for a minute. You're probably looking for ChatGPT. Astra is overkill unless you want to do some damage. I'd stick with GPT-6.0 Terra, not Sol! That one ate through my budget in three days. Terra gets 98.2 on the Enterprise Productivity Benchmark, while Sol gets 99.1. That extra 0.9 will cost you $14,000 a month. So go with Luna if you must.

If you're feeling more adventurous, you could go with Qwen, though. I'd stick with 3.8 MoE. Don't even think about 4 Plus. It's a nightmare. Kimi K is dear to my heart, though. You can't go wrong with it. I use it alongside Codex to complement my workflow. Really great. It scored 91.6 on SWE.
Those are just some of the options.

If you're a programmer, you probably don't need any of that. You just want to use Claude Code. Or get Cursor. Make sure to remove Grok from the auto-selection options. You don't want Grok. If you don't know why, then you don't need to know why.

Anyway, I use Jules with Antigravity now. In VS Code, I use Continue with a local R1 Flash running on Ollama. I use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B for setting up machines, and Qwen-VL to read through my camera feeds. The latter is particularly good at detecting forklifts.
And that's pretty much it. A fairly simple setup, really.

For the layperson, though, it's much easier: they just use the free ChatGPT tier and call it a day... Or Argon. It depends really. Google 3.6 Flash has the lowest score, but it is great for email. I mean how mean do you need your email game to be? Anyway, that's it.
Nano Banana! You probably need that too. It's great with Omni or Carbon. Or wait next week when Hydrocarbon comes out.
That's it!

Here's the one weird trick that made it possible for monopolies to conquer the world: the antitrust bar changed the rules so that it was impossible to prove whether a company had formed an illegal monopoly, and then these rules meant that monopolies were almost never challenged, and what challenges did arise were usually unsuccessful, and even the successful challenges resulted in meaningless "penalties" that left monopolists unscathed.
Every policy has three important dimensions: substance, scope and administrability:
"Substance" is what the policy actually says. For example, the basic substance of copyright law is, "You can't display, transmit or reproduce a copyrighted work without permission."

"Scope" is when the policy gets applied. When copyright law was formulated, the key activities it regulated all required a bunch of expensive industrial equipment. Every book implied a printing press, every record implied a record-pressing plant, every film implied a film duplication lab. That meant that, by default, pretty much the only people who had to care about what copyright law said were industrial actors – firms who might reasonably be expected to also have access to a lawyer. That matters a lot to administrability.

"Administrability" is what it takes to actually administer the policy. Can you detect potential violations, and when you do, how hard is it to figure out whether the rule was actually broken? Again, in the pre-digital era, it was pretty easy to spot copyright violations: pirate books, records and movies are tangible, physical objects, and distributing them requires advertisement, delivery and payment.

After detecting an infringement, copyright enforcers must resolve a further question: whether a display, transmission or copy fall under "fair use." Fair use is a "fact intensive" rule, one that requires a lot of evidence and argument to adjudicate. It's almost impossible to categorically rule in or rule out a specific use as "fair":
https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/27/nuke-first/#ask-questions-never

Despite the complexity and expense of determining fair use, pre-digital copyright was still relatively administrable, because fair use questions themselves were relatively rare. Most fair uses (for example, photocopying part of a book for classroom use) were below the threshold for detection by rightsholders, so these questions almost never found their way into court. The fair use questions that did get to court were big, splashy affairs, like whether it's okay to rewrite a famous pro-slavery novel from the enslaved characters' perspective (it is!):
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Done_Gone

There are a lot of legal questions that require nuance, fact-finding and argumentation to resolve, and that's not necessarily a problem. It's fine to apply these complicated, lengthy processes to things that only happen every once in a while. Take probate: most of us will die one or fewer times, so it's not the worst thing in the world that figuring out what happens to our stuff when that happens can involve some legal complexity.

But as media went digital, copyright's scope expanded dramatically. "Making or handling copies of copyrighted work" stopped being an industrial activity that implied a complex business and access to legal expertise. The only thing a digital computer does is make and handle copies, so every time any ordinary person clicks their mouse, dozens of potentially thorny copyright questions arise. What's more, those questions involve the public internet, which raises the number of potential infringements that a rightsholder can detect (and potentially seek legal redress for) from dozens to millions.

Nearly all of these potential infringements fall under fair use, but fair use is a fact-intensive doctrine suited to resolving occasional disputes between large firms. Fair use is monumentally unsuited to resolving questions that arise hundreds of times every day for nearly every person alive, including small children and other people who almost certainly can't get legal advice:
https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-a-new-deal-for-copyright/

This is how copyright broke: new technology (digital computers) radically expanded its scope, conscripting everyone into using copyright's framework for everyday activities that had nothing to do with the media industry's supply-chain. That framework was developed for industrial actors with access to lawyers, and its most important aspect (fair use) is a fact-intensive doctrine that takes serious work to resolve, but now had to be navigated many times every day by every person. So copyright became unadministrable: you can't apply a fact-intensive doctrine to everyday activities undertaken by everyday people. If you try, you will make criminals of everyone. It would be literally impossible to train enough copyright lawyers to advise every person every time they use a computer to do something that might violate copyright law.

Back to antitrust: when the pro-monopoly partisans of the "law and economy" movement set out to neuter antitrust, they deliberately introduced a set of hurdles that were designed to make it impossible to administer competition law.

First, they introduced an "intent" standard: it was no longer enough for a company to have a monopoly, the company must have intended to secure and maintain that monopoly. If you want to be sure a law doesn't get enforced, this is a fantastic standard to apply. After all, how can anyone know what anyone else intended? Ask any anthropologist and they'll tell you: the only way to find out what someone intends by their actions is to ask them, and even that only works if you can trust them to answer honestly:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thick_description#Clifford_Geertz
If antitrust law can only be enforced by mind-readers and advanced philosophers who have solved the intersubjectivity problem, then antitrust law can't be enforced at all:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersubjective_verifiability

But that wasn't all! Antitrust's enemies insisted on another fact-intensive question: "market definition." They made the (seemingly commonsense) point that if a company is said to have a monopoly, we must first determine which thing the company has monopolized. This sounds like a no-brainer, but it's actually a way to introduce unresolvable, show-stopper arguments into any antitrust enforcement action.

Take Amazon: the company's ecommerce monopoly is obvious to anyone who hasn't been in a coma for the past 15 years. But when Amazon gets investigated for this monopoly, they will insist that they don't participate in the "ecommerce" economy, but rather in "the buying and selling of things in general." Then they point out that people still go to the corner store for a pint of milk, still buy a pack of gum from the kiosk at the train-station, and still buy some hair-gel from the barber after a trim, and therefore Amazon can't possibly have a monopoly.

"Market definition" is a playground for bad-faith semanticians. Luckily for the world's monopolists, the very existence of this legal doctrine has conjured up an army of bad-faith semanticians, most of them with expensive Ivy League economics degrees, who make millions coming up with bizarre market definition arguments that can draw out any legal proceeding for years, often to the point where there is a change in government and the federal prosecutors just walk away from the case.

Taken together, these impossible fact-intensive questions would be enough to bury antitrust, but then came the final blow: frequency. Once capital had won the battle to mire antitrust cases in questions that take years and millions to resolve, they embarked on a frenzy of monopolistic mergers. This meant that the kind of antitrust questions that originally arose every few years were suddenly coming up several times per month. This was the killer combo: making antitrust a plodding ball-ache of thorny philosophical and technical questions, and then rigging the system so that these questions arise in a nonstop flurry guaranteed that antitrust would fail.

That's what happened with Microsoft. The company had a 95% desktop OS market-share when Clinton's trustbusters dragged them into court. Nevertheless, the company played all kinds of "market definition" games that dragged the case out for years. Here's why I think that. Microsoft has demonstrably underinvested in its IT stability. Any IT plan that results in a global, multi-day outage is, by definition, inadequate. Whether the problem could have been solved by buying more servers, or hiring more people, or changing the management of key divisions is immaterial. Did Microsoft need the tens of thousands of workers it threw away? Demonstrably so: when they were on the payroll, Microsoft's servers were up. Now they're gone, and so are the servers. Q.E.D.

This is all characteristic of the monopolist's pathology. The problem with monopolists is that they have pricing power and market power: the power to foist inferior products on their customers and degraded working conditions on their employees and unfair terms on their suppliers. If your company has a dominant position and if it allocates its surplus capital to its investors and if that precedes a significant degradation of your products, then you have an illegal monopoly and you should be broken up. We don't need to inquire as to whether you have a wicked heart that intentionally set about to create a monopoly, nor do we have to argue endlessly about how many angels can dance on the head of your market definition. If you think you are so powerful that you can fuck up your products and not suffer as a result then you are too big to care, and that is simply too big.

This isn't the only fix we need to antitrust law, but it is a fix that would specifically let us target Big Tech. Microsoft is a living, breathing (limping, gasping) repudiation of the thesis that monopolies are efficient and if we only let them amass endless market share and profits, they will use their "economies of scale" to deliver superior products. It's not that economies of scale don't exist, but for companies to take advantage of these economies of scale, they have to be motivated to expend their capital to do so. The more powerful a company is, the less inclined it will be to apportion capital to workers, suppliers and consumers, and the more it will cheat us all to enrich its shareholders.

We can't afford to let this crisis go to waste. Did your company buy another company and then enshittify both products? Great, now we're breaking you up, and your investors are getting fucked. Every policy has three important dimensions: substance, scope and administrability:

The outage lasted for about two days, and around the world, government agencies and businesses large and small ground to a halt. Without Office 365, Outlook and Teams, many organizations could not even convene a meeting or formulate a plan to deal with the outage.

All of this raises an important question: is Microsoft guilty of negligence, and, if so, what should be done about this? Here's my answer: yes, Microsoft is presumptively guilty of negligence, and any response to this must include antitrust breakups of the company.

Here's why I think that. Microsoft has demonstrably underinvested in its IT stability. Any IT plan that results in a global, multi-day outage is, by definition, inadequate. Whether the problem could have been solved by buying more servers, or hiring more people, or changing the management of key divisions is immaterial. Every one of these measures – every single measure that could have prevented this – costs money. By not spending that money, Microsoft definitively underinvested in its products.

But Microsoft doesn't lack for funds! Microsoft is a convicted monopolist, and it has the margins to prove it. In 2025-2026, the company pissed away more than $30b in stock buybacks, a once-illegal (and still sleazy) form of stock manipulation. Over that same period, Microsoft lost nearly $200b on AI ventures that it now admits will not pay off:
https://www.cnbc.com/2025/02/24/microsoft-reiterates-plan-to-invest-80-billion-in-ai-.html
Then there's the layoffs. 2026 saw Microsoft's first-ever voluntary retirement buyout, which served as the overture to a year that saw a 25% headcount cut – 60,000 employees slated for destruction:
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/microsoft-buyout-offers-ai-cuts

Ever had a boss who caught you catching your breath and shoved a broom in your hand, barking, "If you have time to lean, you have time to clean?" That goes quintuple for convicted monopolists who bring the global economy to a halt due to a multi-day outage. If you can't manage to keep your servers online, you have no business incinerating tens of billions on stock buybacks, much less hundreds of billions to feed the AI money-furnace. Did Microsoft need the tens of thousands of workers it threw away? Demonstrably so: when they were on the payroll, Microsoft's servers were up. Now they're gone, and so are the servers. It doesn't matter how those workers related to this specific outage: if you can't keep your servers online, you either don't have enough site reliability engineers, or you don't have enough managers to deploy them effectively, or you don't have enough managers to hire the managers and SREs you need.
Q.E.D.

This is all characteristic of the monopolist's pathology. The problem with monopolists is that they have pricing power and market power: the power to foist inferior products on their customers and degraded working conditions on their employees and unfair terms on their suppliers. Microsoft's hundreds of billions in wastage and tens of thousands of layoffs are a massive transfer of value from customers, workers and suppliers to investors. The fact that the company judged (correctly, it seems) that they could make us all eat shit and we'd ask for second helpings is a nice, clean proof of monopoly power.

Here, I think, is a nice, bright-line, administrable test for monopoly power. If your company has a dominant position and if it allocates its surplus capital to its investors and if that precedes a significant degradation of your products, then you have an illegal monopoly and you should be broken up. We don't need to inquire as to whether you have a wicked heart that intentionally set about to create a monopoly, nor do we have to argue endlessly about how many angels can dance on the head of your market definition. If you think you are so powerful that you can fuck up your products and not suffer as a result then you are too big to care, and that is simply too big.

This isn't the only fix we need to antitrust law, but it is a fix that would specifically let us target Big Tech. Microsoft is a living, breathing (limping, gasping) repudiation of the thesis that monopolies are efficient and if we only let them amass endless market share and profits, they will use their "economies of scale" to deliver superior products. It's not that economies of scale don't exist, but for companies to take advantage of these economies of scale, they have to be motivated to expend their capital to do so. The more powerful a company is, the less inclined it will be to apportion capital to workers, suppliers and consumers, and the more it will cheat us all to enrich its shareholders.

We can't afford to let this crisis go to waste. Google was convicted of creating and maintaining a monopoly three times over the past couple years and every single time the judge decided the company should not face any real punishment for that monopoly, on the basis that the monopoly is what lets Google deliver such excellence for us.

Does anyone still think Google is excellent? How about Apple? Google pays Apple an annual bribe of more than $20b to stay out of the search market. Judge Amit Mehta decided to let Google continue paying this bribe to Apple so that Apple would have the capital it needed to deliver excellent products. Apple promptly went on to have a string of catastrophically bad product launches – while throwing away $170b manipulating its share-price with stock buybacks:
https://finance.yahoo.com/news/apple-dodged-a-20-billion-hit-thanks-to-google-antitrust-ruling-163056806.html

Both companies are demonstrably underinvesting in quality in order to divert R&D and product maintenance capital to their shareholders. They are too big to care. In this age of nonstop mergers and acquisitions, we can't afford to make merger approval turn on fact-intensive questions, but we can sure as hell create this administrable, bright-line test for whether a merger should be unwound after the fact. Did your company buy another company and then enshittify both products? Great, now we're breaking you up, and your investors are getting fucked. Maybe next time they'll fire the board when they announce another stupid, anti-competitive merger.

Microsoft is too big in every way. Too big to fail, too big to jail and too big to care. Too big to trust. Too big to rely upon. Too big to foster a corporate culture that cares about reliability, a decent workplace, or product quality. There's a straight line from GW Bush's decision to let Microsoft skate in 2001 and the situation a quarter century later, where Microsoft is a load-bearing piece of the world's most important firms and government agencies, and where this means that Microsoft knows that it can throw away tens of thousands of workers and hundreds of billions of dollars, crash the planet, and wake up tomorrow unscathed, ready to do it all over again.

blocks.text: The good folks at Thermal Master have sent me (yet another) thermal camera. The P3 Lite has a detachable macro lens. As well as being good for scanning your house for leaks and looking for wildlife, it can focus down on tiny electronic components.
I've previously reviewed their P3 with adjustable macro focus, the chunky T2 Max, and the wildlife spotting DV2 - how does this compare?
Like most thermal cameras, it has a low-ish resolution - 256×192, but their X3 software upscales it to 512×384 running at around 25fps. That's pretty decent for a small plug-in camera.
It also has a magnetically attachable lens for macro-focus, which allows you to see close up details.
You can read the full specs but, basically, it is suitable for all domestic tasks.
Sample Photos and Video
Note, all photos were originally 6MB JPGs - I've losslessly converted them to JPEG-XL and kept the (minimal) EXIF.
Point the camera at something and you'll see which bits are hot. Useful for checking your radiators are working.
Images are stored in portrait mode and have been rotated. As you can see, some of the UI elements remain in portrait mode. Here's a just-finished dishwasher:
A 30 second video is about 12MB - it does include audio from your phone's microphone. I've recompressed and rotated this. It is a tap running cold, then hot, then cold again.
https://shkspr.mobi/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Hot-Water.mp4
Video quality is, I think, excellent.
There are a variety of different thermal palettes to choose from - and the camera excels at spotting where a circuit's hot spots are. Here's a Raspberry Pi:
So what about the macro lens? Here's a close-up shot of a circuit board where I haven't used the included lens:
Not bad, but what if we click the magnetic lens on?
Whoa! Much better. Here's a video demonstrating it.
https://shkspr.mobi/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/lens-on.mp4
Hardware
The camera has a reasonably long USB-C protrusion - so it will fit in your phone even if you use a chunky case.
Because it is USB-C, you can have it facing you or facing away from you. Handy if you want some thermal selfies!
The lens is a simple affair. Note that the protective cover it ships with might not come away cleanly:
I had to prise off the sticker to prevent that residue dirtying the main lens.

It ships with a USB-C extension cable (with USB-A converter) - that's handy if you want to keep camera and phone somewhat separate. It also makes it easy to plug it in to a computer. More on that later.
There's a C to Lightning adapter if you're still stuck on an old iPhone.
Finally, it comes with a little carry case emblazoned with the logo.
The App
The Thermal Master Android App isn't brilliant. It's slow to start and has a bafflingly complicated interface. It takes a couple of clicks to take a photo, rather than the single click you'd expect.

As you can see from the photos, despite the timestamp being rotated, other on-screen elements aren't. You can possibly change this manually in the settings, but it is rather annoying that it doesn't do it automatically. Speaking of which, there are lots of settings to fiddle with - but you'll probably just end up on one that you like and leave it there.
The app does work, but I wish it were snappier.
Linux Usage
There is a Windows App. I couldn't get it working in either VirtualBox or Wine, so here's how to display the camera's feed in Linux.
Plug in the camera via the included USB-C extension cable. It will show up in lsusb as 3474:42b2 Thermal Master Technology Co., Ltd. P2 MAX
Note: the device was previously known as the P2Max and this is reflected in the firmware.
Add a new udev rule with sudo nano /etc/udev/rules.d/99-thermal-p2max.rules
Copy and paste this into the file, then save and exit.

# Thermal Master P2 Max USB Rules
# Allow read/write access for all users
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTRS{idVendor}=="3474", ATTRS{idProduct}=="42b2", MODE="0666"
Reload the rules with sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger
Hurrah! Your Linux machine can now control the camera. There's two ways to view it - and easy way and a hard way.
The easy way is to use https://ferrolho.github.io/thermal-master-viewer/
Open the website in Chrome, click the "Connect camera" button, after a moment you should have a view like this:

The harder way is to use dedicated Linux tools like OpenP3 or Thermal Camera Viewer - you may need to hack around with them so they see the device. Usually that's as simple as adding the PID to the code.
Cost
You're looking at around £220 for the camera and can expect to pay about £40 for the macro lens. You can sometimes find them bundled for slightly cheaper.
Readers of this blog get an extra 6% off at Thermal Master or Amazon UK/US with code THERMLITE6.

Unfortunately, that's pretty cheap for a thermal camera. At that price, I'd recommend buying one to share with your local community. If you are a member of a hack-space, these are invaluable for finding hot-spots on your electronics.

The image quality is excellent. There's no bogus "AI" features to hallucinate what it thinks it saw - you just get the raw image. It would be lovely if it presented as a proper webcam on Linux, but there are open source tools to bridge that gap. The detachable macro lens is handy, and the magnet grip is reasonably strong - but I wish it had a strap or something to prevent it getting lost.
There's not a lot of difference between Thermal Master's various cameras. If you want to swap between wide shots and macro shots, this is probably as good a device as any.

blocks.text: Last time, we figured out  how to pass more than one parameter to co_await by combining the multiple parameter into a single mega-parameter.

But having to name the mega-parameter is annoying. Sure, today we have widget_with_priority, and then we get gadget_with_timeout, and then doodad_with_priority_and_timeout, and oh my goodness it’s out of control.
Instead of making the caller have to name the mega-parameter, we can create a helper method that produces it.
Now callers can write
co_await widget.start(priority);
As a convenience, I gave the start() method a default priority, so you can write
co_await widget.start();
You might even decide to bring back awaiting the widget directly, and having it mean “start with default priority”.
At this point you can simplify the class by just renaming the internal awaitable methods back to their original names.

blocks.text: Since August of 2023, I have been warning that, financially, generative AI might turn out to be a dud.
What if Generative AI turned out to be a Dud?
August 13, 2023

With the possible exception of the quick to rise and quick to fall alleged room-temperature superconductor LK-99, few things I have ever seen have been more hyped than generative AI. Valuations for many companies are in the billions, coverage in the news is literally constant; it’s all anyo…

As I outlined in the very next article after that was that the problem with generative AI was that everyone was following the same path, using very similar techniques, training on very similar datasets. blocks.text: Kepler’s third law
A recent article from Smithsonian magazine says a new dwarf planet candidate is 46 times further from the sun as earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to orbit the sun.
I did a back-of-the-envelope calculation and thought something was wrong. Kepler’s third law says
T² = c a³.
Here T is the orbital period and a is the semimajor axis. If T is measured in years and a is measured in astronomical units (AU) then the proportionality constant c equals 1.
If T = 281.1 years, then a = 42.91 AU, not 46 AU.
Eccentricity

The difference between 46 AU and 42.91 AU is only a contradiction if we assume the dwarf planet is in a circular orbit. The semimajor axis a is the the maximum distance to the center of the orbit, not the distance to the sun. In an elliptical orbit, the focus of the ellipse where the sun sits is not at the center. The orbit is eccentric, meaning off-center.

Assume the dwarf planet candidate ED138 is in an orbit with semimajor axis 42.91 AU. What does the article mean when it says ED138 is “46 times farther from the sun than Earth is”? Does is mean that it is currently 46 AU from the sun, or that its maximum distance from the sun at aphelion is 46 AU? Presumably the latter.

If the distance to the dwarf at aphelion is 46 AU and the semimajor axis is 42.91 AU, then the distance between the sun and the center of the dwarf’s elliptical orbit is c = 3.09 AU. The eccentricity is then
making the orbit more eccentric than that of Saturn but less than that of Mars. This would make the semiminor axis, the minimum distance to the center of the orbit,
The orbit isn’t far from circular, but far enough to account for the substantial difference between the distance to the sun and the distance to the center of the ellipse.

This touches on something that has come up before, and that is eccentricity doesn’t affect the shape of an orbit so much as the position of the sun in that orbit. The orbit of ED138 isn’t far from being circular, but the sun is significantly off-center in that orbit.

blocks.text: A permutation rearranges the elements of a list. The number of arrangements, say of a deck of cards, is finite, so eventually you have to arrive at an arrangement you’ve produced before, and history will repeat itself. Along the way, some cards may move in smaller cycles than others.
Example
For example, consider the permutation
that sends i to p(i). Here indices start with 0.
The number 2 is a fixed point: p(2) = 2. So it has a cycle length of 1.
The number 1 is part of a cycle of length 3: p(1) = 6, p(6) = 3, and p(3) = 1.
The longest cycle is [0, 5, 8, 9, 7, 4] which has length 6.
Longest cycles

What happens to the length of cycles as you permute longer lists? Obviously the longest possible cycle increases with the length of the list, but what happens to the average length of the longest cycle?

Let Ln be the length of the longest cycle in a random permutation of n items. You’d expect the average value of Ln, written E[Ln], would increase when n increases. But do they increase at the same rate? Conceivably E[Ln] goes to infinity as n goes to infinity, but at a slower rate, say proportional to √n rather than proportional to n. Let’s make a plot to see.

There’s a lot of variance, but the central tendency looks approximately linear in n. Let’s repeat our experiment, this time creating 100 random permutations of each size and averaging their maximum cycle lengths.
As we’d expect from the central limit theorem, averaging over 100 samples reduced the scatter by about a factor of 10.

It appears that the expected value of the maximum cycle length grows in proportion to n, and in fact the expected value is somewhere around 0.6n. In the example at the top of the post, the longest cycle is exactly 0.6n. I didn’t plan that: the permutation example was chosen at random.
Asymptotic value
The limit of the ratio E[Ln]/n is known to be

Shepp and Lloyd [1] proved the result above. The constant on the right hand side is known as the Golomb-Dickman constant. I think Golomb investigated E[Ln]/n and had found that there was a limiting value, but Shepp and Lloyd were the first to give a closed-form expression for the limit. Dickman had run into the same constant in a theorem in number theory.
[1] L. A. Shepp and S. P. Lloyd, “Ordered Cycle Lengths in a Random Permutation,” Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 121, no. 2, pp. 340–357, February 1966.
